title: Shankara and the chandala
hookLine: a great teacher says 'move aside', and the man in his path answers back
tomorrow: is there anything in Manu that everyone is asked to keep?

cards: Two people turn in the same assignment late. One gets a zero. The other, the teacher's favorite, gets an extension.
It's hard to sit still after. The Manusmriti has a rule that weighs one act by who did it. And the tradition tells of a morning in Kashi when that kind of weighing got an answer.

teach.b: First the rule. In Manu's eighth chapter, an insult carries a price set by birth.
A kshatriya who insults a brahmin pays a fine, a vaishya a heavier one, and a shudra is punished in his body; a brahmin who insults someone lower pays little. Same words, different price.
That's how the book's justice is built, and it's fair to name it. Now the story.

The tradition tells that the great teacher Shankara was walking by the Ganga in Kashi with his students when a chandala came toward him with his dogs. Move aside, Shankara said. The man answered with questions.
Move what aside? This body of food from that body of food? Or the Self from the Self?
Is the sun different, shining in the Ganga or in a puddle in an outcaste's lane?
Shankara bowed to him. The verses tradition says he made that day, the Manisha Panchakam, say whoever sees the one Self in all is his teacher, whatever his birth.
That's the teaching: the atman, the Self in you, is the same Self in everyone.

The Gita calls the wise sama-darshinah, the ones who see the same in a learned brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and the outcaste who cooks a dog. One rule weighs by birth. One teaching sees one Self.

how: In Hindu study circles that read the Manusmriti critically, its penalties by varna (as in chapter eight) are often read beside Bhagavad Gita 5.18 and the story of Shankara and the chandala told with the Manisha Panchakam.

games.q: two lines, side by side — tap the pairs.

in the story, Shankara bows to the chandala who answered him

Gita 5.18: sama-darshinah, the ones who see the same.

games.q: your manager lets the owner's nephew skip a closing shift you'd be written up for skipping. what move fits today's lesson?
o: ask, calmly, for the same rule for the same act.
accept it; some people simply count for more.
skip a shift yourself, to even things out.
games.why: a critical reader names a double standard plainly. one Self lives in everyone, and the wise see the same; the same act gets the same weighing.

practice: Bring three faces to mind: someone you look up to, someone you barely notice, someone who gets on your nerves. Hold each one for a few slow breaths and say to each, silently: the same Self.
If you pray, you can bow to each in your mind, the way Shankara bowed.

wordCard.voice: The Manusmriti: a law book where the same insult carries a different price, set by birth, read beside the teaching that one Self lives in all.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Bhagavad Gita 5.18: the ones who see the same, the wise.

carryVoice: Hold this close: sama-darshinah, one self in everyone; the wise see the same. Shankara learned it from the man he told to move. Back tomorrow.

sources.ref: Manusmriti 8.267–8.268 (penalties for defamation by the varna of the speaker and of the one defamed)
Bhagavad Gita 5.18 (the wise see the same in a learned and humble brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a dog-cooker)

Manisha Panchakam, attributed to Shankara, with the traditional account of the chandala at Kashi (body of food from body of food, or the Self from the Self; the sun reflected in the Ganga or in an outcaste's lane; refrain: whoever sees thus is my guru, chandala or brahmin)
